text: T-SQL's LIKE only supports simple wildcards — percent and underscore. PostgreSQL adds true regular-expression matching directly as operators. Tilde for case-sensitive regex matching: customer_name tilde caret bracket A B, matching names starting with an uppercase A or B. Tilde-asterisk for case-insensitive matching instead.

PostgreSQL also adds ILIKE — a direct, built-in case-insensitive version of LIKE. Customer_name ILIKE smith matches Smith, smith, SMITH, sMiTh, all of them. None of SQL Server, Oracle, or MySQL have a directly equivalent built-in operator for this.

Now the standout idiom: DISTINCT ON. Select distinct on, customer_id, customer_id, order_id, order_date, from orders, order by customer_id, order_date descending. This returns exactly one row per customer — specifically, their most recent order, because of how you ordered it.

On every other platform in this course, getting that same result needs a window function plus a filter. ROW_NUMBER, partitioned by customer_id, ordered by order_date descending, wrapped in a CTE, then filtered down to rn equals one. Same outcome, noticeably more code.
DISTINCT ON is a real productivity feature worth knowing by name — it's one of the most-cited PostgreSQL-specific conveniences for exactly this latest-row, or first-row, per group pattern.

Regex operators built in, ILIKE for case-insensitive matching, and DISTINCT ON replacing a window-function workaround. Next lesson, the last one in this chapter: translating one real T-SQL query into PostgreSQL, line by line. See you there.
